title: Discussing OpenAI's o1 Strawberry: Unveiling the Next Generation of AI Reasoning — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s central distinction between AI assistance and machine adjudication. It redirects attention to lower-friction AI integration and repackaging AAA’s existing ADR educational content into new formats, while acknowledging that this prospective use had not yet been tested firsthand.
qs: You know, we put a lot of information and classes up online for people who are new to ADR processes, and he was so excited about the ways in which we can put that content out in new forms just by loading it into this tool.
I haven't tried it yet, but I will soon.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source anticipates major legal effects from reasoning AI and recommends selective experimentation and strategic planning, including attention from legal educators. However, it does not address whether automation removes junior work, creates a verification-expertise paradox, or requires reconstructed apprenticeship through simulation, mentorship and independent practice.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: The source aligns with the cluster’s readiness and uneven-adoption themes by urging preparation and forecasting earlier experimentation by in-house teams. However, it does not establish or directly assess the principal proposition that institutional workflow redesign, verification and accountability govern AI’s practical value.
qs: Jen Leonard: I think lawyers should care, probably because—even though we're not going to see Strawberry integrated into legal work this week—lawyers need to know what's coming.
For example, in-house teams that work closely with their business-side partners or clients will probably have to roll up their sleeves and experiment with it sooner rather than later.

st.t: Court AI: Existing failures set the comparison
st.an: The source supports assessing court AI against existing institutional shortcomings and unmet legal need. Its strongest evidence is anecdotal: busy trial judges sought AI assistance for crowded dockets and self-represented litigants whom courts struggle to help. It does not establish effectiveness, and its NotebookLM discussion remains prospective.
qs: But the trial judges were the ones that had their hands up really quickly and basically wanted me, right away, to give them tools to help with their very busy dockets full of litigants who appear without lawyers, both on their end (on the court end, in better handling those busy, long dockets) but more so for the litigants.
They clearly feel that they're just not able to give those litigants the kind of information and help that they might need to understand what's happening and navigate their busy courtrooms.

st.t: Everyday usability: Better formats do not prove accuracy
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s proposition that lower-friction interfaces and new audio formats may encourage everyday legal-AI use, while not proving accuracy or institutional readiness. Its NotebookLM examples are demonstrations, secondhand reports and prospective AAA applications rather than firsthand testing or measured outcomes.
qs: Another cool thing I saw (I didn't experience it myself, but I saw it on LinkedIn) was a demo by Ethan Mollick.
I haven't tried it yet, but I will soon.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: Leonard and McCormack endorse continued practical exploration of AI’s legal, educational and business-model applications without waiting for certainty. Their optimism is explicitly tempered by limited personal testing and reliance on demonstrations rather than systematic evidence, aligning with the cluster’s experimentation-first but reliability-conscious proposition.
qs: Bridget McCormack: I'm happy to talk later about my own attempts to get the most out of Strawberry, which were not very magical—but I think that was a limitation on my part.
Until then, we will continue to explore all of the evolving technology, business models, and educational shifts that we hope generative AI will bring to our profession in the years ahead.

st.t: Professional engagement: Lawyers should shape AI deployment
st.an: The source aligns with the engagement-first proposition by endorsing continued exploration of AI’s legal applications, business models and educational implications despite uncertainty. Its contribution is aspirational and does not add concrete implementation, governance or evidence-based mechanisms.
qs: Until then, we will continue to explore all of the evolving technology, business models, and educational shifts that we hope generative AI will bring to our profession in the years ahead.
Certainly when Orion comes out, we'll have a lot to talk about regarding Strawberry’s application in language and in law.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: The source supports treating legal AI as strategic organisational change rather than immediate, indiscriminate software adoption. It recommends focused team experimentation tied to operations and client needs, combined with forward planning, while anticipating uneven adoption led by in-house teams. It does not materially analyse the cluster’s broader claims about incentives, professional identity, connected data or implementation resources.
qs: Honestly, any law firm, in-house team, or legal organization that’s already thinking about how this technology will change what they do (and how they do it) should assign a couple of people on their team to experiment with it and figure out how it might make a difference for their operations and clients.
It's more about looking forward and planning strategically, rather than fixating on current model limitations and flaws.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source broadly supports selective, staged deployment: it treats legal effects as substantial but not immediate or predictable, urges monitoring and experimentation, and expects adoption to vary by user context, especially among in-house teams and legal operations. Its case is mainly prospective and benchmark-driven, however, and does not materially establish the cluster’s stronger claims about verification, task-level legal performance or operating-model redesign.
qs: Jen Leonard: I think lawyers should care, probably because—even though we're not going to see Strawberry integrated into legal work this week—lawyers need to know what's coming.
For example, in-house teams that work closely with their business-side partners or clients will probably have to roll up their sleeves and experiment with it sooner rather than later.

kp.k: Trial judges seek AI help for unrepresented litigants
kp.d: McCormack reports an anecdotal contrast at Ohio's annual All Judges meeting: appellate judges were skeptical about usefulness for themselves and clerks, while trial judges wanted tools for busy dockets and, especially, to help litigants without lawyers understand proceedings. Few attendees were experimenting, despite strong trial-judge interest. She says this motivated attention within the ABA task force and National Center group; no deployed intervention or measured outcome is reported.
qs: I would say that appellate judges were pretty skeptical that the technology could be useful to them and their clerks
They clearly feel that they're just not able to give those litigants the kind of information and help that they might need to understand what's happening and navigate their busy courtrooms.
So I will say there were not very many judges in the room who were experimenting with the tech yet, but the interest level was so high from the trial judges in the courts with the busiest dockets.

kp.k: Embedded features could reduce friction and encourage adoption
kp.d: Leonard describes Google Workspace replacing a pasted URL with an article title, estimating five or six minutes saved while preparing her monthly newsletter. She explicitly does not know whether the feature uses generative or traditional AI. Both hosts extrapolate that integration into everyday tools, rather than users sorting through models, will support broader adoption.
qs: And I don't even actually know whether it's generative AI or traditional AI
It sped up writing the newsletter by a good five or six minutes, because I didn't have to do all of that manual work in the background.
And I do think that's how we get widespread adoption—when it just inserts itself into your life and makes something easier.

kp.k: Generated podcasts suggest new formats for ADR education
kp.d: Leonard reports seeing Ethan Mollick's NotebookLM demonstration generating a two-person podcast from his book and articles, with accuracy attributed to Mollick rather than independently established. McCormack reports AAA AI-enablement colleague Jason Cabrera's enthusiasm for repackaging introductory ADR information and classes. Both hosts say they have not tried the tool themselves, making this a prospective educational application rather than implementation evidence.
qs: He said that it cited the book accurately.

You know, we put a lot of information and classes up online for people who are new to ADR processes, and he was so excited about the ways in which we can put that content out in new forms just by loading it into this tool.
I haven't tried it yet, but I will soon.

kp.k: Public availability and open source have different implications
kp.d: The hosts distinguish public access through interfaces or APIs from disclosure of code and architecture. Leonard describes open source as enabling modification, redistribution, collaboration and local operation, while associating its practical use chiefly with engineers and technologists. They frame disagreement over openness as involving safety, philosophical commitments and commercial competition, rather than treating public accessibility as equivalent to openness.
qs: Publicly available generative AI tools are tools that are accessible to the general public, either through web interfaces or APIs, but without disclosing or showing the public the underlying model’s architecture or the code that's been used to build it.
Open source is different from publicly available in that the actual underlying code and the model architecture are shared outside of the company that created the technology.
You can also run the code on your own local infrastructure, if you have that capability.
It seems there are some fundamental, philosophical commitments at stake, but there are also commercial, competitive elements to that debate.

kp.k: Hosts frame o1 as a new reasoning-scaling approach
kp.d: Leonard characterizes o1 as strengthening the reasoning process rather than simply predicting outputs, using a math-homework analogy. Drawing on Hard Fork, McCormack presents stepwise reasoning as an additional way to scale models alongside training on more data. These are the hosts' explanatory claims, with explicit acknowledgment that thinking and reasoning terminology anthropomorphizes the technology, not technical findings established in the episode.
qs: So rather than just focusing on the output and guessing, it tries to supervise the process of reasoning out the answer to a question.
(I know we're using words like "reasoning" and "thinking" and anthropomorphizing the tech, but it's the only way to describe it in an understandable way.)
But now they can also scale in another way: by being better and better at reasoning and carefully thinking through a problem.

kp.k: Reported benchmarks emphasize mathematics, coding and scientific reasoning
kp.d: Leonard reports o1 scoring 83% versus GPT-4.0's 13% on an International Mathematics Olympiad qualifying exam and reaching the 89th percentile in Codeforces competitions. She separately attributes PhD-student-like physics, chemistry and biology benchmark performance to a reportedly forthcoming o1 update. Hard Fork stories of problems taking PhDs years but o1 perhaps an hour are secondhand anecdotes. These reports concern technical domains, not measured legal-work performance.
qs: in a qualifying exam for the International Mathematics Olympiad, the new version — the O1 "Strawberry" — scored 83% on the test, compared to GPT-4.0's 13%.
Similarly, in coding proficiency, O1 reached the 89th percentile in Codeforces competitions.
In scientific reasoning, the next update of O1 is reportedly performing similarly to PhD students on challenging benchmark tasks in physics, chemistry, and biology.
I've heard lots of examples—for instance, on the Hard Fork podcast, some PhDs said it took them a few years to figure out problems that O1 can figure out in maybe an hour.

kp.k: Iterative reconsideration illustrates slower reasoning and future model blending
kp.d: McCormack recounts Mollick's crossword example as demonstrating o1's ability to revisit answers rather than remain constrained by an incorrect first guess. The hosts use Kahneman's System 2 as an analogy for slower reasoning. Leonard anticipates companies blending fast responses for simple tasks with more processing time for difficult problems, rather than requiring users to manage that blending.
qs: With Strawberry, though, it could reconsider. It might fill in an answer and then realize something was off and go back to revise.
And that's another way I've been thinking about it—it's like Daniel Kahneman's slow thinking, but done by the model.

We (the users) wouldn't necessarily be the ones doing the blending, but the companies would—so that we can have really quick System 1 answers for things that aren't complicated (like an internet search, for example), and then give the AI more time to think through the System 2-type problems that are really thorny.

kp.k: Immediate benefits for ordinary legal work remain uncertain
kp.d: Leonard considers GPT-4.0 the easier option for most word-based tasks at the time of recording. She says lawyers without technical specialization may not perceive o1's advantage, may find its slower outputs inferior, and may prefer Claude's eloquence. McCormack's unsuccessful attempts to devise challenging tests and an AAA engineer's enthusiasm are personal anecdotes, not evidence of improved legal outcomes.
qs: Right now, GPT-4.0—which we've been using as the most cutting-edge model from OpenAI—remains, to my mind, the easy solution for most tasks we do in a word-based world.

And like you said, in our language-based profession, unless you're in a very, very technical area or you have specialized training, you're probably not going to be able to tell the difference between O1 and GPT-4.0.
I also found it not to be as eloquent as Claude in the way it processes language, but it will be here in our profession soon.

kp.k: In-house teams may face change before law firms
kp.d: McCormack predicts earlier experimentation by in-house lawyers working closely with business partners and by legal operations professionals. Leonard agrees that corporate departments will encounter organizational pressure before law firms, which are one step removed. Their recommendation that firms prepare for clients' earlier exposure is a forecast about adoption pathways, not comparative adoption data.
qs: For example, in-house teams that work closely with their business-side partners or clients will probably have to roll up their sleeves and experiment with it sooner rather than later.
I suspect legal ops professionals will find use cases for it pretty quickly, too.
corporate law departments will feel this sooner than law firms, because those departments will be influenced by the organizations they're part of. Law firms are one step removed from that pressure.

kp.k: Prepare strategically and assign targeted experimentation
kp.d: McCormack recommends that interested legal organizations assign a couple of people to explore operational and client applications, reporting Mollick's advice to spend at least 10 hours rather than 15 minutes. She also recommends involving technically or scientifically trained colleagues and having legal educators consider future combinations of reasoning and existing tools. Leonard takes a more restrained position for most individual lawyers: awareness and strategic planning suffice for now.
qs: Honestly, any law firm, in-house team, or legal organization that’s already thinking about how this technology will change what they do (and how they do it) should assign a couple of people on their team to experiment with it and figure out how it might make a difference for their operations and clients.
Ethan Mollick would say you can't just use it for 15 minutes—you have to use it for at least 10 hours to really see the impact.
In terms of what lawyers should be doing right now, my view is that most lawyers probably don't need to do much with Strawberry yet, aside from being aware that it exists.
I think lawyers (and legal educators) should start thinking about how, when this type of reasoning training is combined with the models lawyers are already using, it could change things.

kp.k: Future legal disruption rests on anticipated capability transfers
kp.d: Leonard predicts substantial legal implications when Strawberry-like reasoning reaches language tasks, while explicitly describing an Orion release built on that technology as rumor. McCormack also anticipates indirect effects as technical advances change client industries and their legal needs. The episode's long-term outlook is optimistic but unspecified in timing and legal applications; it does not establish effects on staffing, fees or service quality.
qs: And rumor has it that OpenAI will be releasing its next language model, which I believe is codenamed Orion, and that model will be built on Strawberry-like technology.
I can't even wrap my head around what it will look like once Strawberry-type reasoning is applied to language tasks in our domain.
And any significant change in an industry will impact the lawyers who help those industries navigate change.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack predict that reasoning-oriented AI will significantly affect legal work when combined with language models, although they do not specify concrete legal performance gains.
pts.d: Leonard describes o1 as an accelerator of AI development and anticipates substantial implications when its reasoning capabilities reach legal language tasks. McCormack argues that AI-driven changes in client industries will also affect the lawyers advising them. These are forward-looking expectations rather than demonstrated legal-service outcomes.

pts.k: In-house departments and legal operations are predicted to encounter useful applications and adoption pressure before law firms.
pts.d: McCormack expects in-house teams closely connected to business colleagues to experiment sooner and legal operations professionals to identify use cases quickly. Leonard attributes earlier exposure in corporate legal departments to pressure from their parent organisations, with law firms experiencing that pressure indirectly through clients.

pts.k: McCormack identifies demand for AI assistance with busy court dockets and self-represented litigants, while asserting that existing tools can already help appellate judges and clerks.
pts.d: Her account distinguishes trial judges' strong interest in court administration and litigant assistance from appellate judges' skepticism. The trial-court discussion establishes perceived need and interest, not proven improvements in access to justice or docket management. Her claim of present appellate usefulness relies on work she references rather than results reproduced in the episode.

pts.k: Embedded AI features are predicted to reduce workflow friction and support widespread adoption.
pts.d: Leonard predicts that everyday software will increasingly anticipate and perform users' routine tasks. McCormack expects adoption to spread when AI makes existing activities easier without requiring users to seek out separate tools. This is a general workflow claim relevant to legal professionals, not a measured sector-wide productivity finding.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal quantitative support for o1's capabilities consists of reported mathematics, coding and scientific benchmarks, not legal-work evaluations.
pts.d: Leonard reports an 83% versus 13% mathematics-exam comparison, an 89th-percentile coding result and anticipated scientific benchmark performance comparable to PhD students. The episode supplies no benchmark methodology or measured legal outcomes. The scientific result is expressly reported for a next update, rather than established as current legal capability.

pts.k: Practical support is anecdotal: judicial reactions, an AAA engineer's experience and Leonard's small workflow time saving.
pts.d: McCormack draws on her Ohio judiciary presentation and an engineer's enthusiasm immediately after o1's release. Leonard reports saving five or six minutes while preparing a newsletter, but explicitly does not know whether the feature was generative or traditional AI. These observations support interest and particular efficiency experiences, not general estimates of legal productivity.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Immediate benefits for ordinary legal language work are qualified; the larger legal implications are expected later, without a firm date.
pts.d: Speaking around o1's initial release in 2024, Leonard says existing GPT tools remain suitable for most word-based tasks. She expects many lawyers to see little difference unless they have technical specialisms, and notes slower output and less eloquent language than Claude. Her expectation of a subsequent Orion model using Strawberry-like technology is explicitly a rumour. For most lawyers, she recommends awareness and strategic planning rather than immediate intensive use.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Courts, self-represented litigants and people unfamiliar with ADR are identified as potential beneficiaries of better information and assistance.
pts.d: McCormack describes trial judges' inability to provide sufficient navigational help to unrepresented litigants. She also reports AAA AI enablement lead Jason Cabrera's excitement about repackaging existing ADR educational material through NotebookLM. The latter is a prospective application reported by McCormack, not an implemented or evaluated service; she says she has not yet tried the tool.

pts.k: Law firms, corporate legal teams, legal operations, educators and technically trained lawyers face preparation and experimentation needs.
pts.d: Leonard urges firms to anticipate changes already reaching clients. McCormack recommends targeted experimentation by people within legal organisations, particularly those with technical or scientific expertise, and asks legal educators to consider the implications of combining reasoning training with existing models. These are recommendations grounded in anticipated change, not findings about job displacement, staffing ratios or pricing.
